structure.heading: Make-versus-Buy Recommendation, Preferred Supplier Criteria, and Contracting Approach (2025–2026)
text_content: **Make-versus-Buy Recommendation, Preferred Supplier Criteria, and Contracting Approach (2025–2026)**

The recommended operating model adopts a hybrid make‑versus‑buy posture: outsource standardized Tier‑1 and Tier‑2 IT managed services while retaining strategic application development and architecture capabilities in‑house. This approach is projected to deliver the target USD 6.3M annual run‑rate savings by Q4 2026 and an estimated 18% reduction in recurring service costs versus FY2024 baseline. Decision factors included risk, IP protection, speed to market, and internal capability uplift and supplier performance expectations.

Supplier selection will be governed by Procurement in conjunction with the Vendor Management Office (VMO) and Legal. The preferred supplier panel will be reduced to 3 suppliers by 30‑Sep‑2025 through a phased consolidation and competitive re‑bid. Criteria emphasize: 1. proven SLA attainment and 99.9% availability history; 2. certified security posture (ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II); 3. competitive total cost of ownership; and 4. demonstrated innovation in automation and tooling capability.

Contracting will implement a 36‑month Master Services Agreement (MSA) with two 12‑month renewal options, executed under centralized procurement and reviewed by Legal and Finance. Key contract terms include explicit SLAs, quarterly KPI scorecards, service credits for non‑performance, and a pricing mix of 80% fixed retainer and 20% variable, KPI‑linked incentives. The MSA will mandate a 90‑day transition plan, defined exit rights, IP assignments, and business reviews through the Vendor Management Office.

structure.heading: Category Spend Baseline and Demand Drivers for IT Managed Services (FY2024–FY2025)
text_content: **Category Spend Baseline and Demand Drivers for IT Managed Services (FY2024–FY2025)**

FY2024 baseline expenditure for IT managed services totaled USD 48.6M. The top three subcategories were Service Desk (USD 14.2M, 29.2%), Network Operations Center (USD 11.8M, 24.3%), and Endpoint Management (USD 9.6M, 19.8%). Supplier fragmentation is notable: 17 active suppliers supporting 112 separate Statements of Work (SOWs) across the estate. This dispersed footprint drives inconsistent SLAs, duplicated tooling, and variable cost-per-incident metrics; baseline metrics will be used to measure FY2025 changes and to benchmark sourcing outcomes.

Primary demand drivers for FY2025 include continued hybrid workplace support, accelerated cloud and SaaS adoption (Microsoft 365, Azure, AWS), and elevated cybersecurity and compliance requirements tied to Zero Trust initiatives. Cost containment pressures from corporate finance target a 5–8% efficiency improvement in run-costs, while transformation programs add incremental demand estimated at 6–9% in service-hours. These dynamics imply simultaneous need for scalable provider capacity, tighter performance metrics, and expandable scope options in future supplier arrangements.

Supply-side considerations for FY2024–FY2025 encompass governance, risk, and commercial simplification. The 17 suppliers and 112 SOWs create administrative overhead, inconsistent risk controls, and impede economies of scale in tooling and training. Consolidation and standardization should be prioritized to deliver savings, tighter control, and vendor rationalization. Proposed actions include: (1) reduce the supplier base to a strategic panel, (2) harmonize SLAs and pricing bands, and (3) centralize contract and SOW templates under joint Procurement–IT governance now.
